Revival of Breakbeat Hardcore which emerged in the 2000s, bringing in modern influences and production techniques.
Minimal sampling, prominent drum machines and Techno elements, and lush synthesizers.
Mixes Hardcore [EDM] with cut-up, complex, and frequently noisy breakbeats at very high tempos inspired by Jungle and Drum and Bass, often with heavy use of sampling.
Heavily distorted or high-pitched Anime vocal samples and complex cut-up breakbeats with extreme tempos.
Sampling, particularly from Pop and Electronic Dance Music, as well as playful melodies, hard kicks, and the typical breakcore breakbeats.
Prominently incorporates samples from Ragga and Dancehall, typically through shouted vocal lines and Reggae-influenced instrumentals.
Combines four-on-the-floor rhythms and hard distorted kicks with the intricate breakbeats, metallic snares, and basslines from heavier Drum and Bass styles.
Aggressive, dark, and often midtempo with influences from Doomcore, Industrial Hardcore, and Nu Style Gabber.
Took shape in the UK in the late 1990s and early 2000s, characterized by rapid rhythms with Gabber-influenced kicks, frequent use of breakbeats and Hip Hop-inspired sampling.
High-tempo fusion of Hardcore Punk and Electronic, combining harsh vocals and electric guitars of the former with electronic instruments.
Typically slower than other subgenres, emphasizing dark, sinister atmospheres, less distorted kicks, droning pads, minimal instrumentation and common use of reverb.
Emerged in France in the mid-2010s, uses French rapping with 4-on-the-floor Hardcore [EDM] and especially Gabber instrumentals.
Emerged in the mid-1990s, combining fast and hard-hitting rhythms with heavy influence from the synthesizers of Trance.
Off-beat, bouncy rhythmic patterns and tempos around the 200 BPM range.
Fast-paced and energetic, often in the 160-220 BPM range, with a hallmark of a distinctive distorted kick sound.
Influences from Hard Trance and Psytrance, creating a melodic and acid-influenced sound.
Emerged near the end of the 1990s; deeper, more harmonic bassdrums with constant use of supersaw melodies, breakdown sections and slower tempos closer to the 150-180 BPM range.

Emerged in the 1990s from the UK Breakbeat Hardcore scene; characterized by saccharine vocals, uplifting piano riffs and spacey effects, gradually developing to emphasize extremely fast-paced four-on-the-floor beats.
Average tempo of 160 to 180 BPM, four-on-the-floor beats, melodic and repetitive synth melodies, drums with hard kicks, short breaks, progressive stomping rhythms, and offbeat notes.
Four-on-the-floor beat around 175 BPM, thick, prominent basslines, and uplifting synth leads, with a cleaner and more accessible sound than other forms of Hardcore [EDM].
Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

Prominent, "stomping", and slightly distorted kick, relentless, repetitive reverse basses on the offbeats (borrowed from Hardstyle) that drive the tracks, giving the genre its distinct energetic sound, and cacophonous, noisy riffs and synth leads.
Heavily associated with Japanese rhythm games, featuring fast melodies and Western Classical Music-derived piano and string instrumentation.
Modern version of the "tribecore" sound featuring deep alternating basses and festival EDM-influenced drops.
Influenced by Reggae, Ragga and Dancehall, combining half-time instrumental sections with Hardtek's fast four-on-the-floor rhythms, as well as vocal samples, clean basslines and skank rhythms.
Forms which incorporate mechanical sound design, high levels of distortion, and dark atmospheres, often at midtempo or fast tempos and commonly based from elements of Gabber, Darkcore and Speedcore.
Exceedingly fast tempos, frequently above 300 BPM, and often aggressive themes and samples.
At and above the threshold of 1000 BPM where sequences of kick drums begin to form a continuous pitch.
Faster version of Speedcore with BPM ranging from around 600 to 1000.
Intense, distorted kicks and rhythms at a fast range of 190-300 BPM coupled with aggressive themes and samples; often presented as a slower alternative to Speedcore.
Utilizes lo-fi production, harsh kicks, and elements borrowed from Rawstyle and other gritty Hardcore [EDM] styles while usually sitting at around 185-220 BPM.
Umbrella term for EDM mainly developed out of Hard Trance and UK Hard House; usually characterized by fast tempos, hard kick drums and a "bouncy" syncopated groove.
Heavily distorted, bass-heavy kicks influenced by Uptempo Hardcore, sustained waves of noise, broader tempo range (130-200 BPM) and a playful contrast between abrasive drops and euphoric melodies.
Hard, four-on-the-floor kick drums, fast tempo around 150 BPM, reverse bass and harsh, distorted synths.
Incorporates the half-time rhythms and wobbly basslines of Dubstep.

Forerunner subgenre that emerged around the turn of the 2000s from Hard Trance and Gabber, distinguished by the signature reverse bass groove, slower tempo around 140 bpm, and straightforward, repetitive sound.
Melodic, more lighthearted, and accessible Hardstyle.

Developed out of Early Hardstyle from the mid-to-late 2000s, by incorporating distorted, crunchy, pitched kicks, faster tempo around 150 BPM, and detuned supersaw/square synth leads playing stompy, dramatic melodies.
Prominent Psytrance influences, especially the basslines and energy of mainstream psytrance.
Incorporates earlier Hardstyle and Hardcore [EDM] influences into the sound of 2010s hardstyle, creating a distinctly harsh, simplistic, raw, and dark sound, with fast BPM.
Combines raw harsh kicks with the uplifting melodies of Euphoric Hardstyle.
Harder, more abrasive, chaotic, and slightly faster variant, with heavily distorted kicks and a focus on experimentation with the kick textures.
Modern version of the "tribecore" sound featuring deep alternating basses and festival EDM-influenced drops.
Influenced by Reggae, Ragga and Dancehall, combining half-time instrumental sections with Hardtek's fast four-on-the-floor rhythms, as well as vocal samples, clean basslines and skank rhythms.
Rave-oriented form of Trance infusing its atmospheres with faster, thumping rhythms and strong melodic / bassline sections, initially spawning out of the first wave in early-1990s Western Europe.
Features a heavy 909 kick drum, four-on-the-floor beat, and a tempo between 140 and 150 bpm.
Dark, dissonant, and minimal, inspired by Techno rhythms; emerged in Northern France in the early 2000s.
Features a "slow and violent" sound between 70-120 BPM with hard kicks inspired by Hardcore [EDM] and Hardstyle.
Revives the sound of late-'90s, early 2000s Hard Dance genres and combines it with Hard Techno drums and structure.
Derived from UK Hard House; featuring darker, more anthemic Trance beats and a tempo of 155-165 BPM.
Emerged near the end of the 1990s; deeper, more harmonic bassdrums with constant use of supersaw melodies, breakdown sections and slower tempos closer to the 150-180 BPM range.
Four-on-the-floor beat around 175 BPM, thick, prominent basslines, and uplifting synth leads, with a cleaner and more accessible sound than other forms of Hardcore [EDM].
Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

Prominent, "stomping", and slightly distorted kick, relentless, repetitive reverse basses on the offbeats (borrowed from Hardstyle) that drive the tracks, giving the genre its distinct energetic sound, and cacophonous, noisy riffs and synth leads.
Defined by offbeat bass patterns, compressed 909-style drums, buildup-drop structures, hoover sounds, and tempos between 120 and 155 BPM.
Features an upbeat and energetic sound often described as being "bouncy", influenced somewhat by Happy Hardcore.
Bouncy hard bass beats, fast tempo, usually 150-175 BPM, and occasional lyrics or rapping.
Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.
Highly percussive, syncopated rhythms, influences from global contemporary genres, and lack of melodic elements, with a tempo lingering around 130 BPM.
German style stemming from Hard Techno and Hardcore [EDM], featuring highly distorted, bass-heavy kicks with snares at each backbeat, often set around 150-200 BPM.
Influenced by Hardcore [EDM] and Techno and made in response to the Vaporwave movement.
Harder, festival-oriented offshoot of Wave, combining its "reese" basses and icy synths with Trap [EDM] drum patterns, build-up-drop structures, and fuller sound influenced by Trance and Hardstyle.
Generally features a four-on-the-floor beat within 110-140 BPM, a groove built on swing and syncopation, synthesized basslines, repetitive melodic elements, and an upbeat mood.
Emerged in the mid-1980s, characterised by repetitive basslines created with the distinctive modulated "squelching" sound of the Roland TB-303 synthesiser.

Emerged by fusing Deep House with Southern African Music, characterized by hypnotizing drum patterns of shakers and congas, often sampled African vocals or soulful original features, and spiritual, organic, melodic atmosphere.
Distinct three-kick-drum rhythm, blends influences from Amapiano and Broken Beat, resulting in relaxed, freeform, playful, Jazz-like feel.
House from South Africa deriving from previous popular genres including Gqom, Kwaito, and Deep House.
Blends the easy-going, poppy, and melodic Afrobeats sound and rhythms with major Amapiano elements, like lush, jazzy, and laid-back atmospheres often featuring light piano chords.
Primarily British genre developed in the 1990s with beats, synthesizers, and vocals in styles similar to House, treated with effects that are often described as "dream-like" or "chilled out".
Hard-hitting rhythms, with generally improvised chanting by commentator MCs and distinctive crash samples; emerged from predominantly Black and LGBT culture in Harlem.
Drew on the "booty bass" syncopation of Miami Bass, combined with Breakbeat rhythms around 130 BPM and chopped up vocal samples as found in Ghetto House.
Busy, punchy percussion, prominent basslines and dirty, distorted synths resembling other bass music genres, with influences including Brostep, Fidget House, Bassline, Speed Garage, and Tech House.
Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.
Strong emphasis on intricate basslines as well as four-on-the-floor beat patterns.
Energetic, festival-oriented style characterized by heavy reverb, intense build-ups, strong kicks, minimalistic drop melodies, and sparse, raw breakdowns.
Originated in the 2010s in Brazil, taking influences from Deep House and Tech House, characterized by deep, punchy basslines making use of detuning and filtering effects.
Blends funk vocal performances with production derived from mainstage 2010s House genres like Brazilian Bass and Slap House.
Late 2010s-born Pop-oriented derivative with prominent, deep "bouncy" basslines and simple, upbeat melodies.
Developed in the Netherlands in the 2000s, combining the older style of Bubbling with more modern House, especially Dutch House.
Emerged in Caracas; highly influenced by 1990s Techno and Tribal House, featuring fast tempos, strident synthesizers, hard-thumping percussion lines, and plenty of breakbeats.
Originated from Chicago around the mid-1990s as a development of Ghetto House, emphasizing hard-hitting, off-beat drum patterns, fast tempos, and lack of melodies.
Distorted, minimalistic TR-909 derived rhythms, basic climaxing structures and heavy reliance on high-pitched synthesizer / hoover sounds.
Umbrella term for a broad variety of House that originated from Chicago in the (mostly mid-to-late) 1980s and early 90s.
Emerged in the United States during the mid-1980s, featuring a relaxed tempo and influences from Jazz, Funk, and Soul.
Nocturnal and nostalgic atmospheres with a distinct dreamy, lo-fi aesthetic.
Dominant, anthemic female vocals, common use of piano stabs, and energetic, driving four-on-the-floor rhythms.
Development of handbag / Diva House characterized by heavier, hard hitting percussion, more pronounced rave and early Hard Dance elements, and fewer vocals.
Warm analog basslines, punchy percussion, crisp high-pitched synthesizer leads, and clipped vocal samples.
Features densely-layered sound design, fast-paced cut-up sections, aggressive stabs, and common crossover with Brostep and Fidget House.
High-pitched wonky synth melodies and heavy influence from Fidget House which developed in the Netherlands around 2007-08.
Blends Dutch House production with Funk brasileiro vocals and drumming on top of Moombahton rhythms.
Makes heavy use of Breakbeat Hardcore-esque synth stabs, pitch bending of basslines, and cut-up vocal samples, as well as glitchy, or "choppy", 4/4 rhythms.
Mixes Electro House with major elements of genres such as Electroclash, Nu-Disco, Synth Funk, and even Electro-Industrial, resulting in a harsh, punchy, and funky midtempo sound.

Offbeat basslines giving it a "bouncy" groove, and minimalistic, side-chained melodies often making use of Dutch House-influenced synths, horns or vocal chops, resulting in a flippant, party-oriented atmosphere.
Blends Funk brasileiro vocals with production from popular late 2000s and early 2010s House.
Vocal-focused style emerging in the late 1980s in Europe, developing in parallel with Eurodance.
Development of handbag / Diva House characterized by heavier, hard hitting percussion, more pronounced rave and early Hard Dance elements, and fewer vocals.

Uplifting, melodic, energetic but clean drops, featuring modern supersaws and pianos, taking influences from Progressive House, Uplifting Trance, but applying them to a form structurally closer to Big Room House and Electro House.
Originated in France in the mid-1990s, characterized by the use of filtered (low-pass, phaser, etc.) samples of Funk and Disco.
Funky, warm, catchy basslines on top of looped Funk or Disco samples, resulting in an upbeat, bouncy, and pacy groove.
Sample-based style influenced by French House and Synth Funk that utilizes Vaporwave editing techniques.
Features distinctive metallic-sounding drops and frequency-modulated basslines at around 120-130 BPM.
Fusion of Melbourne Bounce and Future House that combines the former's basslines and bouncy, upbeat drops with the latter's metallic, pronounced synth leads.
Late 2010s-born Pop-oriented derivative with prominent, deep "bouncy" basslines and simple, upbeat melodies.

Disco-influenced style of House that developed in the 1980s, incorporating elements of Gospel, Soul, and Dub, before evolving into a more upbeat style that prominently features crisp syncopated hi-hats and synth stabs.
Incorporates heavy Gospel elements and singing borrowed from classic and contemporary gospel, usually in the form of choir vocals and call-and-response chants.
Soulful, melodic, Gospel-infused House music developed in Newark, NJ in the late 1980s and early 1990s with an emphasis on songcraft.
Rough sound based around minimal drum machine-driven tracks and heavy usage of vocal samples.
Faster than Ghetto House, playing at 160bpm, and makes striking use of unconventional drum patterns which differ wildly from other House styles.
Deep, dark form of House music that primarily incorporates rap samples or original rapping on top of minimal, bassy beats.
Incorporates production elements of early Hip Hop and usually rapping into 1980s House.
Originated in Italy during the late 1980s, making use of anthemic pianos, diva vocals, and Dance-Pop song structures.
Punchy, 'shuffly' percussion, strong grooves, funky basslines, and chopped-up samples.
Originated in South Africa, utilizing slower tempos and percussive loops alongside laidback chant-like rapping and singing.
Bacardi is a type of House music from South Africa derived from Kwaito, delivering upbeat, danceable rhythms with lively snares and hi-hats.
Incorporates elements of Latin music (various Hispanic American Music and Brazilian Music genres), including their melodies, vocals, and instruments, as well as additional Latin percussion.
Arpeggiated synth lines, focus on a chilled and laid-back atmosphere, and influence from genres such as Progressive House and Deep House.
Stripped-down, minimal form of House, originating in the late 90s, which takes influence from Minimal Techno, Glitch and IDM.
Subtle drums and grooves, slow tempos, and acoustic, traditional instrumentation, resulting in an organic, warm sound and spiritual atmosphere.
Mostly derived from Deep House; intentional use of rough, lo-fi production, often utilizing a mix of analog/analog-like and digital instrumentation.
Nocturnal and nostalgic atmospheres with a distinct dreamy, lo-fi aesthetic.
Merges Drift Phonk's nocturnal atmospheres, cowbell melodies, vocal samples, and energetic production, with House rhythms and tempos, characterized by a banging and upbeat sound.
Trance-influenced strain of House that grew to prominence in the early 1990s, using polished production and gradual progressions.
Short-lived mid-1990s trend with a cinematic, symphonic sound, often with long tracks.
Emerged in the second half of the 2000s in Romania, often featuring brass melodies and "staccato" pluck grooves.
Primarily British style that paved the way for UK Garage, combining cut-up vocal samples and sped up four-on-the-floor Garage House rhythms with Jungle-esque basslines.
Emerged in the 2020s taking influences from Melodic House, Trance, and Future Garage; features distinctive chopping of vocal samples and pads.

Emerged in the mid-1990s taking influences from Techno, broadly characterized by minimalistic and repetitive melodies, focus on the bassline, and constant groove recognizable by prominent off-beat hi-hats.
Incorporates UK Garage rhythms and synths stabs, influences from British rave music, UK Bass and UK Deep House, resulting in an urban, subdued, but danceable sound with deep, muted basslines.
Hypnotic, minimal, and "dubby" loops, featuring subtle and intricate synth pads, cranky, clicky percussion, and bouncy, pulsing basslines.
Prominent, syncopated rhythms of tribal drums such as toms and bongos on top of a House beat, usually resulting in a percussive, energetic sound, while ranging in mood.
Originated in Colombia, featuring "fluttering" trumpets, accordion, and tambora drums.
Offshoot of Deep House featuring slow tempos around 100-115 BPM, light percussion and acoustic instrumentation, setting out to create a relaxed, summery, beach-like atmosphere.
Defined by offbeat bass patterns, compressed 909-style drums, buildup-drop structures, hoover sounds, and tempos between 120 and 155 BPM.
Features an upbeat and energetic sound often described as being "bouncy", influenced somewhat by Happy Hardcore.
Bouncy hard bass beats, fast tempo, usually 150-175 BPM, and occasional lyrics or rapping.
Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.
Successor to British Bassline, characterized by strong basslines, dark atmospheres, and dominant grooves.
Fast-paced House popular in Vietnam, remixing Vietnamese melodies.

Emerged in the 2020s by mixing fast tempos, prominent basslines, and hard-hitting drums derived from popular Techno with simplistic, catchy melodies and vocals, often influenced by 2000s Hard Dance, Eurodance and Electropop.
Exaggerated fast form of Belgian Techno for the Japanese market, focusing mainly on synth sounds and samples typical of 1990s dance music.

Emerging mostly from Dutch House and Big Room House, incorporates Tribal House-influenced percussion, hard kicks, and animal sounds resulting in a wild, jungle-resembling atmosphere in a festival EDM-oriented context.
Bitcrushed synths and occasionally bitcrushed vocals, energetic Jersey Club-derived beats, and elements of Sigilkore's dark production style.
Angolan music combining traditional Kilapanga and Semba with Techno and House.
Initially developed in the late '80s in Luanda, Angola, as a mixture of Soca- and Zouk-based percussion samples.
Spanish Techno developed in the early 1990s; strongly influenced by New Beat and EBM, but aiming for a lighter sound.
Asian Electronic Dance Music that mixes vocals and melodies from Mandopop with fairly hard, melodic EDM.
Outgrowth of Melodic Dubstep with euphoric sound design taking influences from Future Bass, guitar melodies and Pop-driven structures.
Harsh synth leads and a usual tempo of around 90-110 BPM.
High-pitched synth leads, gritty percussion, a kick-snare pattern, aggressive bass drops, and around 110 BPM while often paralleling Complextro or Brostep.
Offshoot of Dutch House characterized by tempos in the 100-110 BPM range, Reggaetón-influenced rhythms, bass-heavy kicks and high-pitched synths.
Stylistically diverse form of underground Japanese Electronic Dance Music utilizing energetic beats built around samples from pop and/or nerd culture.
21st-century trend mixing modern, polished Electronic production with the aesthetics, structures, and lively, organic beats of 1970s and 1980s Disco.
Incorporates elements of Moombahton and Dubstep to create a style characterized by sluggish, kick-heavy dembow rhythms.

Early, dominant form of Synthwave that developed from French Electro and Electro House in the late 2000s; features fast, driving beats, melodic synth leads, nocturnal atmosphere, and heavy evocations of 1980s pop culture.
Minimalistic, atmospheric sound design and eclectic drum patterns, derived from but not fitting Dubstep.
South African genre with very fast BPM (around 180) featuring MIDI keyboard sounds and marimba.
Developed in Tanzania in the mid-2000s; fuses incredibly rapid beats, usually between 180-300BPM, with MCing and musical influences from older Tanzanian genres.

Mid-2000s offshoot of the Nordic Electro scene which uses simple, analogue or Chiptune-inspired synthesizer leads and basslines to create stripped-down, midtempo grooves drawing on Synth Funk and Hip Hop.

Loud synth leads with a distorted, gritty, and "slimy" sound design, usually laid on top of production inspired by or taken directly from genres such as Halftime, Trap [EDM], Brostep, and other forms of 2010s EDM.
Highly beat-driven, repetitive, and mechanical, typically featuring minimal chord variation and melodies, focuses on rhythms and timbral variety; generally produced for club environments.
Incorporates "squelching" synths from Acid House into a mechanical and usually more energetic Techno context.
Blends the mechanical, repetitive beats of Techno with atmospheres and textures inspired by Ambient music, resulting in slower tempos and more understated rhythms.
Early form of Hardcore [EDM], resulting from the further evolution of New Beat due to the strong influence of Techno and EBM.
Established in the late 1980s in the breakdancing and early rave scene of Yorkshire in the North of England, notable for its "bleepy" synth lines and heavy sub-bass.
Features a signature mechanical, detached sound that echoed the atmosphere of Detroit's nightlife and incorporated influences from Electro and Chicago House as well as Synthpop and Electro-Disco.
Originated in the early 1990s, commonly played at free parties in Europe, and features a repetitive pounding kick drum at tempos of 170 BPM or above.
Features shuffling grooves with heavy emphasis on layered percussive elements; often includes a mix of samples and drum machines played at a range of 135-140 BPM.
Typically rave-oriented form characterized by hard, prominent kick drums, pounding rhythms, fast tempos around 140-160 BPM, and aggressive, often distorted sounds.
Characterised by fast tempos, aggressive "whooshing" beat patterns, heavy compression and straightforward song structures.
Harder, darker style of Techno which draws parallels with factories and the rhythm of machinery.
Cold, mechanical, and hypnotic tracks, typically lacking the harsher and noisier elements of later Industrial Techno.

Trance-influenced subgenre that was established in the mid-to-late 2010s, characterized by gradually progressing structure, and hypnotizing, atmospheric sound with arpeggiated, minor melodies, playing at around 120-125 BPM.
Stripped-down and sparse, often featuring a dark sound and a slow, steady development through the track.
Incorporates atmospheric delay and reverb effects derived from Dub with an emphasis on live mixing.
Emerged in the early 2000s as a variant influenced by Trance melodies, structures, and progressions while retaining hypnotic basslines and repetition, with a tempo between 122 and 130 bpm.

Hard, dynamic, energetic, and accessible subgenre featuring strong kicks, massive dirty synths, tempos around 130 BPM, more suspenseful structures with breaks and buildups, and a big, modern, festival-oriented sound; rose to high popularity in the late 2010s.
Emerged in the late 1990s and early 2000s; grew out of a combination of Techno and EBM.
Strays from the standard beat of Techno, opting for a more fractured sound.
Minimal, stripped-down with an emphasis on low-frequency bass partitions.
Slow and minimalistic extreme form, focused on ultra-low frequency sine wave notes and mainly intended for stress testing subwoofer sound systems.
Blend of the themes and singing style of Rumba flamenca with the most commercial forms of House, Techno, and Makina.
Incorporates samples from children’s television series, public information films and Children's Music over Breakbeat and Techno-inspired beats with a lighthearted and nostalgic disposition.
Evolving, tension-building structures with rapid, minor arpeggios on top of a hypnotic, four-on-the-floor drum patterns at fast tempo around 130-150 BPM.
Incorporates "squelching" acid basslines into Trance's evolving structure.
Inspired by Balearic Beat and Mediterranean relaxing atmosphere, with a tempo of around 130 bpm.
Incorporates production features associated with Big Room House and dirty, distorted leads influenced by Electro House, Dutch House and Hardstyle.
Slow tempo (about 130 BPM) with strong roots in Progressive House, using beats typical of Eurodance and Dance-Pop; emphasizes a laid-back, carefree, and dreamlike sound.
Incorporates prominent, dirty saws from Electro House, evolving from Tech Trance and emerged in the 2000s.
Emerged as a fusion with Eurodance, features fast tempos, more accessible grooves and structures, and simple, catchy melodies with vocals and saw synth leads.
Prominent, melodic supersaw leads, Dance-Pop derived hooks, and a strong reliance on sidechained basslines and hard, powerful drums.
Japanese style that emerged in Shibuya's club scene in the 2000s and was primarily marketed to gyaru, infused with melodic and rhythmic influence from Eurobeat.
Rave-oriented form of Trance infusing its atmospheres with faster, thumping rhythms and strong melodic / bassline sections, initially spawning out of the first wave in early-1990s Western Europe.
Largely Japanese genre with an energetic and glitchy sound derived from Full-On Psytrance and Complextro.
Derived from UK Hard House; featuring darker, more anthemic Trance beats and a tempo of 155-165 BPM.

Combines Progressive House and early Trance; emerged in Western Europe in the early to mid-1990s featuring gradual development, atmospheric textures, restrained energy, and subtle melodic progression.
Emphasizes a psychedelic feel and an energetic sound; based around influences from Goa Trance and Acid Trance.
Uses more complex sound design based on dark atmospheres and fast tempos.
Glitchy sound design, morphing synth lines, strange sounds typically evoking futuristic or alien-like atmospheres, and faster tempos than most other forms of Psytrance.
Pushes the dark atmospheres of Dark Psytrance to the extreme through the usage of exceptionally high tempos and experimental soundscapes influenced by Dark Ambient and Glitch.
Mimicks the ambience of a forest by using swarming and teeming effects as well as natural samples; features straightforward song structures.
Faster and more intense, usually set around 145-150 BPM and featuring harder rolling basslines, vocal samples and "spacey" effects.
Forerunner of Psytrance styles that emerged in the early 1990s, distinguished by old-school, organic sound with rapid, oriental-inspired melodies.
Fast-paced, featuring rapid melodic lines and usually hard and high-pitched kicks.
Emerged in the early 2000s, featuring a slow tempo range and clean production.
Experimental and leftfield approach to Progressive Psytrance, mixing the atmospheric and clean Psytrance production typical of it with funky and jazzy elements.
Finnish-based deviation of Psytrance with an emphasis on free-form experimentation and humor.

Late 1990s-emerging subgenre characterized by energetic percussion with loud kicks, filtered hi-hats and tribal drums; side-chained, detuned and repetitive leads, as well as other raw, distorted, and complex sounds influenced by Techno, Hard Trance and Electro House.
Features euphoric climaxes similar to Festival Progressive House while keeping its Trance-oriented structure and atmosphere, often with Electro House-influenced intros.
Euphoric melodies, buildup-breakdown-anthem structures, common usage of supersaws, and a BPM range of usually around 135-142.
Melodic, polished, Pop-like, and vocal-focused with around 120-145 BPM and frequent overlap with Progressive Trance, Uplifting Trance, and Euro Trance.
Trap-influenced syncopated percussion with 808 samples and fast-paced hi-hats.
Massive, sub-bass-heavy drops with simple melodies, synth leads and production influenced by Big Room House; highly popular from 2013 to 2015.
Often abrasive and heavily influenced by Hardstyle.

Blends Trap [EDM]’s signature percussion and sub-basses with euphoric, uplifting, melodious drops prominently derived from Festival Progressive House, contrary to the gritty, "dirty" nature of other EDM trap styles.

Blends deep 808 kicks, hard-hitting sub-bass and rolling hi-hats with major influences from heavy bass music genres, and in particular, metallic, gritty, and off-kilter sound design, originally derived from Brostep.
Fast-paced; draws influence from Bounce and Miami Bass.
Percussion from Cumbia and Mexican Folk Music with upbeat Electro House-derived production and fast, triplet-oriented rhythmic patterns.
Prominent bass/sub-basses, a deep, dark, airy, and mechanical sound derived from Dubstep, and eclectic production influenced by UK Funky, Juke/Footwork, Techno, and Breakbeat.
Influenced by UK Garage-related styles and the regional styles of British immigrants, including Soca and West African-inspired Tribal House.
Syncopated, shuffling rhythms at 128-140 BPM, emerging in the mid-1990s from Garage House with additional influences including Jungle and Contemporary R&B.
Lacks 4-on-the-floor kick patterns, resulting in jittery rhythms; features deeper basslines and relaxed atmospheres.
Strong emphasis on intricate basslines as well as four-on-the-floor beat patterns.
Hard-hitting Breakbeat rhythms and heavy, rolling basslines.
Stripped-down, bass-heavy, atmospheric style drawing influence from Dub and Drum and Bass; served as a precursor to Dubstep.
Combines the rhythms of late 1990s and early 2000s 2-Step with novel moods and production approaches, commonly featuring jittery, broken rhythms, vocal chops, and warm synth pads and plucks.
Primarily British style that paved the way for UK Garage, combining cut-up vocal samples and sped up four-on-the-floor Garage House rhythms with Jungle-esque basslines.
Off-kilter fusion of Dubstep and Hip Hop which first developed in the mid-to-late 2000s.
Syncopated, half-time rhythms inspired by Dubstep and Grime, funky, sludgy, "aquatic"-sounding synths and sound design.
Dense, layered, and compressed production, usually coupled with a distinct fuzzy and "warm" low-frequency synthesizer style.
Cinematic, dense digital collage; frequently utilizes a Deconstructed Club sonic palette and decontextualized novel samples.

Fast-paced short sounds, complex structures with erratic progression, and often dense and atmospheric abstract sound design, featuring recontextualized elements from IDM, Speedcore, Industrial Hardcore, and Breakcore.
Combines sound design techniques from IDM and Glitch with acoustic instrumentation inspired by Contemporary Folk.
Originated in eastern North America around the turn of the 21st century, combining trends of Synth Funk and Italo-Disco.
Uses abstract sound design and malfunctioning electronics—CD skips, data corruption, and hardware noise—as main compositional elements.
Incorporation of IDM-derived production into drum patterns inspired by Hip Hop beats.
Compositional technique in which markings are manually applied to a medium, then processed by a machine to produce synthetic sound from the markings in real time.
Heavily bit-crushed, sometimes sped-up and pitched-up vocals, and highly compressed, distorted production, typically using preexisting material from other genres.
Bitcrushed synths and occasionally bitcrushed vocals, energetic Jersey Club-derived beats, and elements of Sigilkore's dark production style.
Combines eerie and haunting synth pads and sharp, abrasive sounds to create atmospheres that accentuated the dark, unnerving, violent, or ghostly themes of horror films.

Developed and took inspiration from Bubblegum Bass and popular 2000s-2010s Electropop, characterized by eclectic, unconventional, mechanical-sounding and dense production; and by manipulated, usually auto-tuned vocals.
Emerged through the development of Electronic Dance Music idioms into a less club-oriented and more experimental direction, often incorporating unconventional sound design and complex rhythms.
Frenzied, intricate beat programming inspired by Drum and Bass.
Combines Ambient soundscapes with Hip Hop drum patterns, breaks, and samples through the busy effect layering of Dub.
Leftfield or DIY approach characterised by simpler Pop-informed melodies, often incorporating vocals or live instrumentation alongside Electronic production.
Emulates vintage aesthetics and popular musical styles of the 1980s/1990s altered by modern recording technology to create a hazy dreamlike atmosphere.
Mixes Synthwave with major Chillwave elements, characterized by a dreamy and relaxed sound.
Incorporates elements of more experimental Electronic styles like IDM and Glitch.
Originated in the early 2000s as an offshoot of the Japanese Shibuya-kei movement when artists introduced more prominent "bleepy" electronic elements and faster tempos.
Combines Electronic with Latin American influences; started at the end of the 1990s.
Emerged in Caracas; highly influenced by 1990s Techno and Tribal House, featuring fast tempos, strident synthesizers, hard-thumping percussion lines, and plenty of breakbeats.
Mixes an Electronic sound into traditional Cumbia through influences from House, Dancehall, Hyphy, and Dubstep.
Mixes elements of Merengue and Reggaetón with polished production from mainstream House subgenres; often shares traits with Latin Pop, having anthemic melodies and verse-chorus structures.
Combines Tango rhythms and melodies with Electronic music.
Samples and synthesizes Mexican styles like Banda sinaloense and Norteño into a sound related to IDM and House.
Percussion from Cumbia and Mexican Folk Music with upbeat Electro House-derived production and fast, triplet-oriented rhythmic patterns.
Incorporates Electronic instrumentation into live Rock jamming, drawing on a wide variety of Electronic Dance Music and Downtempo styles.
Combines the 6/8 ternary rhythm with Electronic production, using computer music, synthesizers and drum machines.
Arrangement of microsounds on an incredibly small time scale.
Retrospective term for more Electronic and minimal forms of New Wave, Post-Punk, Synthpop, and related styles, tending towards a more sparse and lo-fi sound.
Minimal and distinctly DIY take on Synthpop with a bleak and naive aesthetic.
Moog synthesizer-led music often associated with a wave of Novelty records in the 1960s and 1970s.
Based around the technique of speeding and pitching up pre-existing songs.
Electronic styles which feature aesthetics and occasionally instrumentation inspired by Jazz.
Waves of feedback, screeching analog synthesizers, and harsh, screamed vocals.
Combines the abrasive textures of Noise and Industrial music with dark, brooding drones and atmospheres.
Combines looped samples of Noise with Electronic rhythms.
Synthesizer-driven genre focusing on developing, often longform compositions and drawing inspiration from various sources such as Progressive Rock, Western Classical Music, and Ambient.
Atmospheric, multilayered synthesizer textures; pioneered in Berlin in the 1970s.
Flowing and relaxing synthesizer-based music derived from Progressive Electronic, often oriented around imagery of outer space.
Led by melodic synthesizer sounds, often with reverberating drum machine patterns; commonly associated with the 1980s.
Derivative of EBM, retaining its apocalyptic worldview but incorporating heavy influence from the melodic style of Synthpop.
Heavily influenced by Electro-Disco, featuring cheap "electronic organ" synth leads and minimalistic, repetitive rhythms.
Offshoot of 1980s Kayōkyoku and Idol kayō incorporating characteristics from Synthpop.
Appropriates the harsh elements of Punk Rock but replaces the predominance of guitars with synthesizers and drum machines.
Rooted in 1980s synth music, characterized by large, throbbing "retro" synths and visual elements, often features upbeat percussion and/or epic, cinematic atmospheres.
Mixes Synthwave with major Chillwave elements, characterized by a dreamy and relaxed sound.
Incorporates atmospheric Horror Synth and faster tempos into a much heavier and darker sound.
Gentle, relaxed and downtempo with emphasis on uplifting melodies, lush soundscapes and breathy, reverbed vocals.

Early, dominant form of Synthwave that developed from French Electro and Electro House in the late 2000s; features fast, driving beats, melodic synth leads, nocturnal atmosphere, and heavy evocations of 1980s pop culture.
Fast and electronic-based style that evolved from Brega calypso, particularly associated with peripheral areas of the city of Belém.
Raw and vulgar Tecnobrega and Funk brasileiro fusion developed in the late 2010s by DJs in Belém do Pará.
Meta-genre beginning with the rise of Vaporwave and the aesthetics that it spawned.
Borrows elements from Downtempo, Trip Hop, and Instrumental Hip Hop; emulates 1990s and 2000s Chillout music.
Accentuates ambiance and a dreamy, futuristic atmosphere, taking influence from Progressive Electronic, as well as Cyberpunk and Dystopian movies.
Sample-based style influenced by French House and Synth Funk that utilizes Vaporwave editing techniques.
Influenced by Hardcore [EDM] and Techno and made in response to the Vaporwave movement.
Emulates late 20th century futuristic and corporate aesthetics, often using "tacky"-sounding instruments likened to MIDI Music, in contrast to Vaporwave's sample-based approach.
Uses Noise and other avant-garde techniques not typically found in Vaporwave.
Incorporates a blend of Trap percussion set to the re-utilization of old samples, such as 1990s pop culture or old computer library sounds.

Sample-based, involving heavily synthesized and processed manipulation of corporate mood and background (elevator) music, though source material can also include Pop, Contemporary R&B, and Synth Funk.
Manipulates samples from TV broadcasts, advertisements, film, radio, and other sources.

Simple, prototypical Vaporwave style, heavily influenced by Chopped and Screwed and Glitch, that features short, slowed-down, lyric focused, sampled loops smothered in reverb and continuously repeated, usually taken from late 20th century music.
Evokes shopping malls by utilizing heavy reverb and sampling styles commonly used as mall background music such as Easy Listening and Smooth Jazz.
Utilizes a distinct form of sample manipulation to create a “slushy” sound, usually sequenced in soft Ambient-based soundscapes.
Melancholic, atmospheric, melodic beats, defined by its Trap and Cloud Rap influence, ethereal and cold production style, and abundant use of sub bass.
Harder, festival-oriented offshoot of Wave, combining its "reese" basses and icy synths with Trap [EDM] drum patterns, build-up-drop structures, and fuller sound influenced by Trance and Hardstyle.
Mixes Wave with Grime and other forms of UK Electronic music.
Nocturnal, occult-themed/horror-inspired, and murky beats with altered, slowed down and heavily processed samples laid on top of slow Hip Hop-derived drum rhythms and droning, dense synthesizers.
Collective improvisation directed by a conductor.
Usage of data to create sound, soundscapes and music mostly as a way to illustrate its information.
Focuses on long, sustained tones and tone clusters, or repetition of single notes.
Manipulation and processing of sound sources to create atmospheric pieces.
Fixed-media Electroacoustic music designed to be reproduced by multiple loudspeakers without the presence of instrumentalists and visual cues.
Improvised, slow-moving, abrasive, and makes use of silence and extreme frequencies; performed with unconventional combinations of objects, prepared instruments, and electronics.
Manipulation of recorded sounds, mostly Field Recording, natural sounds, and real-world noises, as a process of abstracting "concrete" sounds, or "sound objects", from their acoustic origins.
Employs electronic technology to incorporate sound directly into the process of composing poems.
Improvised music which, in descending from Free Jazz and classical Indeterminacy, further abandons the prescriptions of harmonic or rhythmic structures which characterized those genres.
Radical and militant attitude, rejection of Western Classical Music and traditional criteria of craft, non-conformity, and a fascination with machines.
Uses abstract sound design and malfunctioning electronics—CD skips, data corruption, and hardware noise—as main compositional elements.
Compositional technique in which markings are manually applied to a medium, then processed by a machine to produce synthetic sound from the markings in real time.
Leaves elements of composition, performance, or both up to chance.

Emerged out of punk and avant-garde art movements in the mid-1970s, often characterized by a bleak, mechanical atmosphere, the use of metallic percussion as well as other unconventional instruments, and extensive use of sampling influenced by Musique concrète.
Waves of feedback, screeching analog synthesizers, and harsh, screamed vocals.
Combines the abrasive textures of Noise and Industrial music with dark, brooding drones and atmospheres.
Arrangement of microsounds on an incredibly small time scale.
Style of semi-improvisation that derives heavily from both the composition of Modern Classical and the techniques of Avant-Garde Jazz.
Acoustic, through-composed Classical Music that relies heavily on unconventional instrumental techniques.
Strays away from conventional structure, tonality, and composition and consists predominantly of noise.
Soft, sparse textures inspired by the static composition of Harsh Noise Wall.
Incorporates unconventional sounds with overpowering or constant Noise and Black Metal elements, often being heavily texture-oriented, abrasive, dissonant, atonal, or repetitive.
Combines and subverts Goregrind and Grindcore with brash Noise and even faster drum tempos.
Highly aggressive walls of sound that assault the listener.
Quick and dynamic form made from rapid cuts between various sounds.
Harsh, distorted walls of sound that feature few dynamic variations and often take the form of long compositions with little to no change or progression over time.
Waves of feedback, screeching analog synthesizers, and harsh, screamed vocals.
Combines the abrasive textures of Noise and Industrial music with dark, brooding drones and atmospheres.
Combines looped samples of Noise with Electronic rhythms.
Compositional technique of utilizing and manipulating one or more recognizable recordings to create a new composition.
Quiet dynamics and use of silence, often in the extreme.
Small, unassuming sounds, usually created by amplification and manipulation of recordings of quiet phenomena.
Exploration of the physical traits of sound rather than music as expression.
Incorporates elements from Experimental music and visual arts, with sound utilized as its primary medium and subject.
Compositional method emphasizing the rough layering of sampled elements, presenting an impression similar to a visual collage.
Cinematic, dense digital collage; frequently utilizes a Deconstructed Club sonic palette and decontextualized novel samples.
Focuses heavily and often exclusively on phonemes and sub-phonemic sounds, rather than semantic meaning.
Employs electronic technology to incorporate sound directly into the process of composing poems.
Explores the nature of audio recorded to magnetic tape and the act of playing sound from it.

Has its roots in the early half of the twentieth century, with experimental artists using the turntable (as well as the vinyl records it plays) as a distinct instrument in the creation of compositions.
Generally acoustic and rooted in modernized Traditional Folk Music; originated with the 20th-century American folk revival.
Blends avant-garde and neo-classical compositions with traditional Country Blues fingerpicking techniques.
Rawer approach to folk, with an often self-mocking and sarcastic tone.
Experimental-influenced and playing with instrumentation, rhythm, and other factors not commonly found in folk.
Incorporates improvisation, repetition and extended song lengths.

Born in Taiwan in the mid-1970s, this movement originated with university students creating their own modern-style songs in the wake of international tensions like Taiwan's isolation from the United Nations and the United States' embrace of the PRC as a diplomatic partner.
Gentle fingerpicked acoustic guitar or harp-led music that commonly includes a backing ensemble of harpsichords, strings, horns, or other orchestral instruments.
Emphasises Traditional Country instrumentation as well as influences from contemporary Singer-Songwriter traditions, such as a gentler disposition and prominent lyrical storytelling focus.
Originated in England in the early 1960s, featuring a distinctive guitar fingerpicking style of the same name and the DADGAD guitar tuning.
Blends Contemporary Folk with a Pop sensibility, most popular in the late 1960s and early 1970s and featuring influence from the contemporary Folk Rock style.

Highlights driving "stomping" rhythms and shouted group vocal harmonies, often drawing influences from Pop Rock, Indie Folk, and other genres, while maintaining a characteristically mellow and commercial sound.
Combines the melodic sensibilities and production style of Indie Rock and Indie Pop with acoustic instrumentation and influences from Folk, Singer-Songwriter, and sometimes Country.

Highlights driving "stomping" rhythms and shouted group vocal harmonies, often drawing influences from Pop Rock, Indie Folk, and other genres, while maintaining a characteristically mellow and commercial sound.

“Life-oriented” style of Bengali-language music, defined by socially conscious and often politically-charged lyricism, as well as its incorporation of elements from Contemporary Folk and Bengali Folk Music.
Lo-fi, downbeat, and frequently depressive atmosphere with psychedelic undertones that emerged among independent creators following the collapse of the counterculture in the 1970s.
Emerged in the mid-1980s from the Post-Industrial scene, with a dark, often martial atmosphere.
Minimalistic and melancholic sound with influence from Nordic Folk Music and even Ambient.
Short-lived movement that reincorporated traditional Chilean folklore into modern production and styling inspired by foreign musicians.
Draws from a variety of sources to subvert traditional acoustic song forms, with diversity ranging from Jazz to Medieval music to various Regional Music traditions.
Acoustic forms that capture an atmosphere that is at turns dream-like, 'spaced-out', whimsical, haunting, mystical, and melancholic.
Loosely defined 2000s Psychedelic Folk revival closely associated with the New Weird America movement, sometimes also a shorthand for certain leftfield styles of psychedelic and Indie Folk.
Incorporates improvisation, repetition and extended song lengths.
Movement that emerged in the Brazilian city of Recife during the 1970s that combines psychedelic elements with music of Northeastern Brazil.
Closely tied to mysticism, old folk beliefs, and Folk Horror; often described as 'witchy' or 'pagan.'
Grew out of British Trad Jazz, drawing influence from 1920s Jug Bands and the strong rhythms of 1950s Honky Tonk and Rock & Roll.
Singaporean Mandarin-language style, generally featuring harmonised group vocals and backed mainly by acoustic guitar.
Informed by a long history of tradition in a specific culture or region, mostly associated with the peasantry and non-aristocratic public.
Indigenous music of Africa that is passed down orally from generation to generation, the authors of the songs are usually unknown.
African Folk Music developed by the Yabassi people of Cameroon.
Yoruba Music developed by Muslims during the late 1930s and early 1940s in the Ijebu region of Yorubaland, the current Ogun state.
Tradition from Cape Verde, unusual among the islands' music due to its lack of polyphonic singing and its usage of polyrhythms.
Music of the Dagomba people of northern Ghana.
A mystical musical tradition centred around the qraqab castanets and guembri bass lute, named after its originators, the Afro-Maghrebi Gnawa people.
Traditional Folk Music of the Kabye people of northern Togo, including some of the most singular styles that can be found in West Africa.
Tradition of the Bakongo people from Angola and Congo that has influenced contemporary styles such as Kuduro.
Melodic, chordophone-dominated sound; based on the Austronesian Music of the first settlers that arrived on the island from Borneo.
Music of the Mbenga and Mbuti people, Pygmy ethnic groups in Central Africa.
Tradition that originated in Seychelles among Creole slaves, similar to Séga, although rawer and played only on large flat drums made from goatskin.
Played in Swahili-speaking African countries; primarily focused on rhythm.
Danceable triplet-based genre from the coastal regions of Kenya and Tanzania.
Traditional music from Zanzibar, traditionally played at women's initiation rituals and weddings.
Traditional Folk Music of southern Africa.
Musical traditions developed by the Afrikaner community in southern Africa.
Encompasses traditions of the Khoisan ethnic family groups.
Traditions of the Nguni ethnic family groups, a southern Bantu ethnicity.
Traditional Folk Music of the Sotho-Tswana ethnic family groups from southern Africa.
Tradition from the central region of Benin around Savalou, played with water percussion.
Derived from Traditional Séga, this is the original dance music of La Réunion.
Séga dance music born in the 18th century, before its later adoption of Western pop elements.
Energetic, percussive style based around a large, heated drum known as a tambour, traditionally popular on Rodrigues and the Chagos Archipelago.
Traditional rhythmic chanting and percussion adapted to multiple West African contexts in the 20th century.
Traces back through the history of European and West African settlement and migration to North America, including parts of northern Mexico and Canada in addition to the United States.
Folk of the Appalachian Mountains in the Eastern United States.
Various styles of Blues originating in the rural US South, typically relying on expressive vocal delivery and featuring simple, usually acoustic instrumentation.
Laid-back swing rhythms and guitar ornamentation, including solos.
One of the earliest forms of Blues, named for the Mississippi Delta region of the United States where it developed, with a highly rhythmic style and a typical 12-bar structure.
Brooding, hypnotic minor-key open-tuning guitar style with a looser structure, often featuring high, "haunting" vocals.

Emphasizes a steady hypnotic groove, sparse percussive and highly energetic guitar riffs, and often features meandering structures with unconventional and usually fewer chord changes compared to Delta Blues.
Developed in the early 20th century in the southern Appalachian foothills and characterized by a syncopated but melodic Ragtime-based finger-picking acoustic guitar style.
Created by African-American slaves working on cotton plantations, featuring expressive vocals to no strict rhythm.
Rooted in martial Fife and Drum Corps music, originated among Afro-American communities in Mississippi.
Usually features a jug as the bass instrument as well as other homemade (or easily affordable) instruments, such as kazoos and washboards.
Pre-Bluegrass North American string band styles, particularly those rooted in Appalachian Folk Music.
Traditional music of the Pennsylvania Dutch.
Ritual practiced by African-Americans in the US South, characterized by shouting, chanting and people dancing in a circle while praying and clapping.
Four-part harmony Christian singing tradition popular in the American South, using singing books such as the Sacred Harp.

African American folk song based around Christian themes, originating during enslavement and emphasizing solidarity and freedom; musical features include call-and-response, "blue" notes, and expressive vocal timbres.
Adaptation of sacred African-American folk song to formalized written arrangements for concert performance, informed by Western Classical Music conventions.
Energetic call-and-response vocal harmonies with complex rhythmic syncopation, delivering themes of liberation after hardship through Biblical stories.
Solo voice and piano arrangement of sacred African-American folk song, drawing on the form of German Lieder to guide an expressive concert performance.
American Folk Music with spoken or nearly spoken vocals; often features dry humor and social commentary.
Earliest and most "pure" form of Cajun Music, employing basic rhythms and frequent fiddle double stops.
Closely aligned with American Folk Music and Blues roots, from country's inception in Appalachia and the American South until the popularity of Honky Tonk and Country Pop in the 1950s.
Traditional two-part harmony singing performed mostly by brothers.
Incorporates the harmonies and Christian themes of Gospel.
Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.
Vocal technique of Yodeling, brought to the United States by German settlers, sung over the instrumentation of Traditional Country.
Driving tempos, acoustic stringed instrumentation, and high vocal harmonies, adhering to the stylistic roots of the Bluegrass genre.
Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.
Traditional Folk Music of the Arabic people.
Arabic Folk Music from rural Morocco with piercing singing, scratchy viola, and rollicking hand drums.
Accompaniment to traditional belly dances.

Tempo between 130 and 160 BPM, played with keyboards and metal instrumentation, sung with harsh and aggressive vocals including many clean melodic styles; regularly uses elements of Melodic Death Metal, Symphonic Metal, and Electronic Dance Music.
